title: A Scene in Shantytown, New York
credit: New York Daily Graphic, 4 March 1880 · Stephen H. Horgan
note: Widely cited as the first halftone photograph printed in a newspaper. Zoom in: there is no grey anywhere on the page — only dots of varying size, printed at a ruling coarse enough to survive newsprint.

title: Frederic Eugene Ives
credit: Ives Process Co., New York · published 1905
note: Ives (1856–1937) patented the first commercially successful halftone process in 1881 — a process that used no screen. The crossline screen he is remembered for came later.

title: Georg Meisenbach
note: Granted German patent 22244 on 9 May 1882 for Autotypie — single-line screens rotated during the exposure to produce a crossed effect.

title: The first Autotypie
note: Meisenbach's first autotype plate, trimmed irregularly. One of the earliest surviving relief halftones made for commercial printing.

title: Sixty, seventy-five and eighty-five lines
credit: The Half-Tone Process, Iliffe & Sons, London · 1904
note: The same photograph of the Flatiron Building, printed through three coarse Levy screens. Newspaper rulings: the dots are visible at arm's length.

title: One hundred and seventy-five, two hundred, four hundred lines
credit: The Half-Tone Process, Iliffe & Sons, London · 1904
note: The same building again, through fine screens. At four hundred lines the dot structure has left human vision entirely — which is the whole objective.

title: High lights to half-tones
note: A continuous tonal ramp photographed through a screen. Watch the dots grow from nothing.

title: Half-tones to shadows
note: The other half of the ramp. Past fifty per cent the dots touch and invert: what was a grid of ink becomes a grid of white holes in a solid field.

title: One portrait, three screens
note: Unscreened, then at 130 lines, then at 175. The argument for fine rulings, made in the only medium that can make it.

title: Screen and plate holder
note: The glass screen sits in clips at a measured distance from the plate. That gap is what turns a ruled grid into round dots of varying size.

title: Screen adjustment and a process camera
note: Linley's patented screen-adjusting camera back, with handwheel, and the full bellows process camera it was fitted to.

title: Plate-making frame
note: Brass corners, screws, hinged plate glass — drawn as a line engraving, because in 1904 that was still how you illustrated a manual about printing photographs.

title: Impressio Librorum
credit: Jan Collaert I after Stradanus · Nova Reperta, ca. 1600 · The Met, CC0
note: The invention of book printing. Compositors at the type cases, the great screw press mid-pull, printed sheets hung to dry — the machine that could not print a photograph for another three hundred years.

title: Sculptura in Aes
credit: after Stradanus · Nova Reperta, ca. 1600 · The Met, CC0
note: The invention of copper engraving. Engravers cutting plates by hand at the window, a star-wheel rolling press behind them.
